**Embodiment is seasoning. One or two per page.** *"A page that reacts to
everything feels haunted, not alive: the visitor stops reading and starts
poking, which is the opposite of what any of this is for."* Pick the one that
serves the peak and leave the rest.

These are gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` — a pointer-capability
query, which stands.
Upstream also turns them off under reduced motion — **that half utgår, F-011**.
The rule that does survive is upstream's own:
*"a technique that only exists on desktop cannot be the thing that carries the
page's meaning."*

## Pacing as emotion

Upstream `feel.md` § 5. *"Scroll distance is emotional time. It is the only
clock this medium has, and it is fully under your control, which makes it the
cheapest emotional instrument in the kit and the one most often left at
default."*

| Pacing | Reads as | Built with |
|---|---|---|
| Short acts, hard cuts | Adrenaline, pulse, impatience | Acts under 1.4 vh, no `pin`, `dwell` at 0 |
| A long pin | Held breath, pressure, attention | `data-sc-span` 3+, overlapping cues, one idea |
| An empty viewport before a reveal | Silence before the drop | A ground-only act, no cue until the next one |
| A slow settle mid-act | The shot landing | `data-sc-dwell` 0.35–0.6, cue peak on the settle |
| A fast cue with a long plateau | Confidence, arrival | `data-sc-cue="0.1 0.9 0.08 0.4"` |
| A slow ramp in | Hesitation, dawning | Long `rampIn` — **once per page**, it is close to feeling broken |

Four rules follow:

- **Silence must be authored, not left over.** *"An empty screen you meant
  reads as anticipation. An empty screen you did not mean reads as a page that
  failed to load, and the harness reports both as dead scroll."* If the empty
  viewport before the peak is deliberate, **say so in `BRIEF.md`** so the
  verification pass can tell it from dead scroll. This is the sentence that
  keeps `scroll_verify.py`'s `blankBands` check from being either useless or a
  false alarm.
- **Give the peak room.** The peak act has the largest span on the page by a
  visible margin. *"If every act is 2.2 vh, the page has no shape, whatever
  the curve in BRIEF.md says."*
- **Compress the administrative parts.** Specs, logistics, FAQ, credentials
  are information, not experience — flow sections at short stagger, never
  pinned acts with dwell. Spending scroll on them spends the visitor's
  patience on the part they will not remember.
- **A continuous world is the exception to pacing variety.** All of the above
  is about a page of *acts*. A worldflight is one camera move, and *"a camera
  that changes speed between legs reads as broken rather than as
  expressive."* There, hold one pace and let the peak carry the shape by being
  the single long leg — [`pace.md`](pace.md).

The total-length budget stays **8–14 viewport-heights**. Pacing is how that
budget is spent, not permission to spend more: *"a page that needs 20 vh to
land its curve has too many acts, not too little room."*

## The fingerprint gate

Registry: `VAULT/wiki/projects/_index/design-fingerprints.md`, per-vault,
starting from whatever rows already exist — not repeating **yourself** across
builds, not a universal constraint. **Six dimensions**, recorded per row:

| # | Dimension | What it records |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grammar | Which of `grammars.md`, or a named new one |
| 2 | Nav treatment | What the chrome is and what it's for |
| 3 | Hero device | What the first screen does |
| 4 | Act-sequence shape | Device order, act count, total viewport-heights |
| 5 | Close pattern | How the last screen behaves, what the CTA sits in |
| 6 | Signature move | The one bespoke interaction, in a phrase |

**The gate: a new build must differ from EVERY existing row on at least 4 of
the 6** — four against each row individually, not averaged across the table.
Dimension 6 is free (unique by definition), so the gate really asks for 3
more out of the remaining 5 against each row. If the plan fails, **change
the plan, not the log** — rewriting a row to fit is what makes it worthless.

**Row format** — one row per shipped build, all six dimensions plus a world
note and the path: `| Build | Grammar | Nav | Hero device | Act-sequence
shape | Close pattern | Signature move | Register | World / palette | Path |`

**Rows are append-only.** From upstream `templates/FINGERPRINTS.md`:

> *"A build that has been superseded stays in the table, because the space it
> occupies is still occupied."*

A replaced, retired or rejected build keeps its row. The registry does not
record what is live; it records what surface has already been taken, and a
surface stays taken whether or not the build that claimed it is still up.
Deleting a row silently frees a shape for reuse, which is the same failure as
editing one to make room — *"never edit a row to make room for it. If a
planned build fails, change the plan."*

**Fill every column.** A row with blanks cannot be scored 4-of-6 against, so
it weakens the gate for every build after it.

**Keep a "what is taken" list beside the table.** Add a bullet whenever a
build claims something a later build should avoid reusing: a grammar, a nav
treatment, a close pattern, a signature move, an act-count-and-length band.
*"The shared columns are what the next build inherits as a constraint, so
writing them down is the whole point."*

After shipping, append the row and say what it shares with prior rows — the
shared columns are exactly what the *next* build has to avoid.

1	# Motion smoothness — why a page that renders correctly can still look cheap
2	
3	Anton, r7 (FEEDBACK.md F-012): *"scrolleffekten renderade som den skulle, men det såg
4	hackigt och billigt gjort ut."* The measured answer is F-013. Read this before writing
5	any scroll-driven motion, and read it again before "fixing" motion that someone has
6	called janky — because **two different faults produce that same sentence**, and the cure
7	for one does nothing for the other.
8	
9	## The two faults
10	
11	| | The value steps | The page drops frames |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| What you see | Motion advances in visible notches | Motion stutters and lags the hand |
14	| What the clock says | 60 fps, nothing wrong | frame p95 well over 20 ms |
15	| Where it comes from | A raw scroll value written 1:1 | Too much work per frame |
16	| What fixes it | Damp the value (`--sc-ps`) | Cut the work (`performance.md`) |
17	
18	Measure both before changing anything: `scripts/motion_probe.py` reports frame time and
19	value continuity in one run. Guessing which fault you have is how a session spends an
20	afternoon smoothing something that was never stepping.
21	
22	## Fault 1 — the raw value
23	
24	`scrollcraft.js` damps exactly two things: the video playhead (lerp 0.18, deadband,
25	seek coalescing) and the pointer devices `tilt` / `magnet`. Its own docstring explains
26	why: *"wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate and a 1:1 write reproduces every
27	gap in them."*
28	
29	That reasoning is right, and the engine does not apply it to `--sc-p`. Everything
30	`read()` writes — `--sc-p` itself, cue opacity, parallax, pan, kinetic units,
31	`clip-path`, drift — is written 1:1 from raw scroll position, on the scroll event
32	behind a one-frame rAF guard. On a mouse wheel the value stands still between notches
33	and then jumps.
34	
35	Two things make it worse:
36	
37	- **`--sc-p` is an unregistered custom property.** To CSS it is a string, so it never
38	  interpolates, and no `@property` registration exists anywhere in the engine.
39	- **`scrollcraft.css` sets `transition: none`** on `[data-sc-cue]` and `[data-sc-copy]`
40	  once `.sc-ready` lands. That is deliberate — JS owns the value — but it means nothing
41	  bridges the gap between two writes.
42	
43	**F-011 did not cause this.** `var reduce = false` turned the playhead lerp *on*
44	(rate 1.0 → 0.18). `reduce` gates ten sites in the engine and every one is a disable
45	branch. The stepping is architectural and predates the override.
46	
47	### The rule
48	
49	> **Bespoke motion reads `--sc-ps`, never raw `--sc-p`, whenever it drives something the
50	> eye sees move** — `transform`, `object-position`, `clip-path`, `mask-position`,
51	> `background-position`. Cue opacity may read `--sc-p`.
52	
53	`--sc-ps` is published by `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js`, copied in beside the engine and
54	loaded after it. The engine is never edited (`scroll/NOTE.md`: copy, never edit). The
55	shim lerps at 0.16 per frame with a 0.0005 deadband, registers `--sc-ps` as a real
56	`<number>` so CSS can interpolate it, stops its own rAF loop when nothing is moving, and
57	sets `will-change` **only while an act is actually in motion** — correcting the engine
58	CSS's seven class-level promotions, which `motion.md` § Bans forbids.
59	
60	A page's own rAF painters (`paintHeroPool`, `paintMotion`, a word scrub) read `--sc-ps`
61	too. `?preview=` modes set `window.__scFreezeMotion = true`, and the shim then tracks the
62	raw value exactly so a screenshot shows the formed state, not a lerp in flight.
63	
64	Measured, same motion, same wheel cadence (`tests/motion/`):
65	
66	| | frame p95 | staircase | largest single-frame step |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| `staircase.html` (raw `--sc-p` → `rotateY`) | 16.7 ms | 18 | 5.6 % |
69	| `smooth.html` (lerped) | 16.7 ms | **0** | **1.4 %** |
70	
71	The frame clock is identical in both. The difference is entirely in the value.
72	
73	## Fault 2 — the page is genuinely slow
74	
75	Damping a value on a page that cannot hold 60 fps just makes a smooth curve arrive late.
76	V3b, measured 2026-09-08 with no CPU throttling at all: frame p95 49.9 ms, 62 frames over
77	33 ms, 4.9 MB transferred, 19 font files, 17 long tasks during scroll, four elements with
78	a resting `will-change`. See `performance.md` for the budget and `scripts/perf_probe.py`
79	for the measurement.
80	
81	## Pace — the third thing people call "not smooth"
82	
83	From upstream scroll-craft's `worldflight.md` § 7c, the only place in the corpus where
84	someone diagnosed the complaint to root cause: *"Two separate faults get described as
85	'it doesn't feel smooth', and only one of them is smoothing."*
86	
87	- **Inconsistent pace is the worse one.** Across a multi-act or multi-leg sequence,
88	  `rate = weight / seconds` must hold within a few percent. On the `orrery` build it
89	  varied 36 % across ten legs and the owner's word for it was "not smooth"; evened to
90	  6 %, the same footage read as one continuous move.
91	- **Too fast reads as cheap.** For a fly-through, 0.21–0.22 vh per second of film is the
92	  floor. The per-8-seconds guardrail is a dead-scroll floor, not a taste target.
93	- **Damping and weights fix different halves.** *"The damping is what removes wheel
94	  judder; the weights are what remove the surging."* For a worldflight use
95	  `data-sc-lerp` **0.12**, not the 0.18 default, and widen `data-sc-seam` to ~0.16.
96	
97	`motion_probe.py` reports `max_step` per act, so an act that surges relative to its
98	neighbours shows up as a spread across runs rather than as a feeling. Full port, with
99	the weight arithmetic and the worldflight knob values: [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).
100	
101	## The bar
102	
103	A signature act is not finished until, at 4× CPU throttling:
104	
105	- `staircase = 0`
106	- `max_step ≤ 3 %` of the value's own range
107	- frame p95 ≤ 20 ms, zero frames over 33 ms
108	- both scroll directions measured, not just downward
109	
110	## What the harness still cannot tell you
111	
112	Upstream's `verify.md` says it plainly: *"Whether the motion is smooth. Contiguous frames
113	prove the clip advances; they do not prove it advances evenly."* `motion_probe.py` closes
114	most of that gap and does not close all of it. Watch the contact sheet for a move that
115	lurches, reverses, or stalls in the middle, and watch the sparkline the probe writes: a
116	curve with a flat shoulder is an act that stops dead mid-travel, which no single number
117	reports.
118	
119	One known, accepted inconsistency: `scripts/scroll/scrollcraft.css` line 98 still carries
120	`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { html { scroll-behavior: auto } }`. It only
121	disables smooth anchor jumping and touches no act, and the engine is never edited, so it
122	stays — documented here rather than silently tolerated.
123	
124	## Related
125	
126	[`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) · [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md) ·
127	[`performance.md`](performance.md) ·
128	[`motion.md`](motion.md) · `scripts/motion_probe.py` · `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js` ·
129	FEEDBACK.md F-011, F-012, F-013.

| | The value steps | The page drops frames |
|---|---|---|
| What you see | Motion advances in visible notches | Motion stutters and lags the hand |
| What the clock says | 60 fps, nothing wrong | frame p95 well over 20 ms |
| Where it comes from | A raw scroll value written 1:1 | Too much work per frame |

  interpolates, and no `@property` registration exists anywhere in the engine.
- **`scrollcraft.css` sets `transition: none`** on `[data-sc-cue]` and `[data-sc-copy]`
  once `.sc-ready` lands. That is deliberate — JS owns the value — but it means nothing

branch. The stepping is architectural and predates the override.

> eye sees move** — `transform`, `object-position`, `clip-path`, `mask-position`,
> `background-position`. Cue opacity may read `--sc-p`.

loaded after it. The engine is never edited (`scroll/NOTE.md`: copy, never edit). The
shim lerps at 0.16 per frame with a 0.0005 deadband, registers `--sc-ps` as a real
`<number>` so CSS can interpolate it, stops its own rAF loop when nothing is moving, and
sets `will-change` **only while an act is actually in motion** — correcting the engine

| `staircase.html` (raw `--sc-p` → `rotateY`) | 16.7 ms | 18 | 5.6 % |

Damping a value on a page that cannot hold 60 fps just makes a smooth curve arrive late.
V3b, measured 2026-09-08 with no CPU throttling at all: frame p95 49.9 ms, 62 frames over
33 ms, 4.9 MB transferred, 19 font files, 17 long tasks during scroll, four elements with
a resting `will-change`. See `performance.md` for the budget and `scripts/perf_probe.py`
for the measurement.

From upstream scroll-craft's `worldflight.md` § 7c, the only place in the corpus where

'it doesn't feel smooth', and only one of them is smoothing."*

  `rate = weight / seconds` must hold within a few percent. On the `orrery` build it

  6 %, the same footage read as one continuous move.

prove the clip advances; they do not prove it advances evenly."* `motion_probe.py` closes

curve with a flat shoulder is an act that stops dead mid-travel, which no single number
reports.

stays — documented here rather than silently tolerated.

## Related

[`scroll/devices.md`](scroll/devices.md) · [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md) ·
[`performance.md`](performance.md) ·
[`motion.md`](motion.md) · `scripts/motion_probe.py` · `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js` ·

content.content: 1 # Performance — the budget, and what spends it 2 3 Until 2026-09-08 the chain had one line about performance and no script, no budget and no 4 gate. The cost showed up as taste: a page that drops frames during scroll gets called 5 "hackigt och billigt" (F-012), which is the same sentence a stepping value gets, and the 6 two need opposite fixes. Measure with `scripts/perf_probe.py`; read 7 [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md) for the other half. 8 9 ## 1 · Budget (gate 93) 10 11 Measured locally through `scripts/serve.py`, real Chrome, `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate 12 4`, no network throttling, at 1440×900 and 390×844. 13 14 | Measure | Limit | Why that number | 15 |---|---|---| 16 | LCP | ≤ 1.8 s | ≈ 2.5 s in the field, the Core Web Vitals floor | 17 | CLS | ≤ 0.05 | Metric-matched font fallbacks plus `aspect-ratio` on every image make 0 reachable; 0.05 is margin | 18 | Long tasks (> 50 ms) during scroll | **0** | A long task under the thumb *is* the jank | 19 | Frame time during scroll | p95 ≤ 20 ms, none > 33 ms | 60 fps with headroom | 20 | Transfer at 1440 | ≤ 2.5 MB total | V3b shipped 4.9 MB | 21 | Hero image | ≤ 250 kB WebP | It is the LCP | 22 | Fonts | ≤ 3 files, ≤ 300 kB | V3b shipped 19 files / 732 kB | 23 | DOM | ≤ 1500 nodes | Single-file HTML | 24 | Resting `will-change` | 0 elements | Promotion is for motion in flight, not for standing still | 25 | `filter` / `backdrop-filter` on > 50 % of the viewport | 0 | GPU repaint per frame during scroll | 26 27 **A scrubbed clip has its own line and does not count against the page budget:** 28 ≤ 32 MiB for all desktop clips, ≤ 16 MiB for all mobile clips, fetched as a Blob *after* 29 first paint so it never sits on the LCP path. A clip loaded in the fold breaks both 30 budgets at once. 31 32 ## 2 · Loading 33 34 - **Every ``**: `width` and `height` attributes (both — the single largest cause of 35 layout shift), `decoding="async"`, `fetchpriority="high"` on the LCP image, 36 `loading="lazy"` below the fold, `srcset`/`sizes` when it renders under 60 % of the 37 viewport width. 38 - **The hero must be vendored.** Downscale to ~2200 px on the long edge, re-encode WebP, 39 commit it. It must not depend on another company's CDN — measured 2026-09-08, V3b's 40 heaviest resource was a 1.1 MB hero hotlinked from `images.unsplash.com`, which is both 41 a budget failure and a Step 5b rule violation nobody had caught by eye. 42 - **Fonts**: `.woff2` only; `` for the display 43 weight that appears in the fold, and only that one; `font-display: swap`; a 44 metric-matched fallback `@font-face` (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, 45 `descent-override`) so the swap costs no shift; one variable file once you need three 46 weights or more; `font-weight` as a property, never `font-variation-settings`; 47 `-webkit-font-smoothing` set once on the root, never per element. 48 - **Iframes**: `loading="lazy"` *and* mounted by an `IntersectionObserver` about one 49 viewport ahead. Three live iframes mounted at load is the heaviest thing a marketing 50 page can do to itself. 51 - **`content-visibility: auto`** with `contain-intrinsic-size` on long sections below the 52 fold. It is the cheapest single win on a twelve-act page. 53 - **preconnect** to any origin the fold actually needs. 54 55 ## 3 · Rendering 56 57 - **Animate `transform`, `opacity` and `filter`.** Everything else costs layout or paint 58 per frame. `clip-path` composites only in newer Chromium — treat it as a paint cost 59 elsewhere and keep the animated area small. 60 - **`will-change` only while the element is moving**, removed at rest. Setting it 61 class-wide promotes every match to its own layer for the life of the page, which is 62 itself a jank source on a mid-range GPU. `sc-smooth.js` corrects the engine's own 63 class-level promotions at runtime. 64 - **Blur is expensive in proportion to area.** `backdrop-filter` only on fixed or sticky 65 chrome, never on a full-bleed surface during scroll. Grain film goes on a fixed, 66 `pointer-events: none` pseudo-element at 4–5 % so it is painted once. 67 - **`transition: all` is a defect**, not a shortcut: it animates properties you never 68 meant to animate, including layout-triggering ones, and retargets on every change. 69 - **No layout reads in a scroll handler.** One passive listener that only schedules, one 70 rAF loop that reads and writes, a deadband so the loop stops when nothing moves. The 71 engine's own shape is the model; `window.addEventListener('scroll')` doing 72 `getBoundingClientRect()` per event is the anti-pattern. 73 - **`min-height: 100dvh`, never `height: 100vh`.** The iOS address bar changes `vh` 74 mid-scroll and the act jumps. 75 - **Isolate a continuous animation in a leaf element** so it cannot force its parent to 76 re-render. 77 78 ## 4 · Motion 79 80 Timings, easings and the ban list live in [`motion.md`](motion.md); the smoothness rules 81 and the `--sc-ps` contract live in [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md). The 82 performance-relevant half: 83 84 - Transitions retarget from their current value; keyframes restart. For anything a user 85 can interrupt, use a transition. 86 - A scrubbed clip needs a **dense GOP** or it seeks like mud — see 87 [`assets.md`](assets.md) § Encoding. A normal web encode places a keyframe every two to 88 five seconds and plays back perfectly while scrubbing terribly. 89 - Stagger at 30–80 ms and cap the number of staggered items; a cascade of forty is forty 90 animations. 91 92 ## 5 · Measuring 93 94 ```bash 95 python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/serve.py --port 3000 --root . 96 python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/perf_probe.py --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/page.html --cpu 4 --out shots/perf 97 python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/motion_probe.py --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/page.html \ 98 --track "#hero:--sc-p,#hero:--sc-ps,.plate-card:transform" --out shots/perf 99 ``` 100 101 Never `python -m http.server`: it is HTTP/1.0 and drops large WebP responses under 102 Chromium on Windows, so you end up measuring a page that failed to load. 103 104 Both probes are proven in both directions before they are trusted — 105 `tests/perf/{heavy,clean}.html` and `tests/motion/{staircase,smooth}.html`. A check that 106 only ever fires is as useless as one that never does: if a probe flags a known-good 107 reference build, it is over-greedy and gets narrowed, not waived. 108 109 ## 6 · Never 110 111 - A hero image on someone else's CDN. 112 - `transition: all`. 113 - `will-change` on a class. 114 - A blurred surface larger than half the viewport, animated during scroll. 115 - More than three font files, or a preload for a weight that is not in the fold. 116 - An iframe mounted at load. 117 - A scroll handler that reads layout. 118 - `height: 100vh` on a full-height act. 119 - Shipping a number from this file that you did not measure on the actual page. 120

file.content: # Performance — the budget, and what spends it Until 2026-09-08 the chain had one line about performance and no script, no budget and no gate. The cost showed up as taste: a page that drops frames during scroll gets called "hackigt och billigt" (F-012), which is the same sentence a stepping value gets, and the two need opposite fixes. Measure with `scripts/perf_probe.py`; read [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md) for the other half. ## 1 · Budget (gate 93) Measured locally through `scripts/serve.py`, real Chrome, `Emulation.setCPUThrottlingRate 4`, no network throttling, at 1440×900 and 390×844. | Measure | Limit | Why that number | |---|---|---| | LCP | ≤ 1.8 s | ≈ 2.5 s in the field, the Core Web Vitals floor | | CLS | ≤ 0.05 | Metric-matched font fallbacks plus `aspect-ratio` on every image make 0 reachable; 0.05 is margin | | Long tasks (> 50 ms) during scroll | **0** | A long task under the thumb *is* the jank | | Frame time during scroll | p95 ≤ 20 ms, none > 33 ms | 60 fps with headroom | | Transfer at 1440 | ≤ 2.5 MB total | V3b shipped 4.9 MB | | Hero image | ≤ 250 kB WebP | It is the LCP | | Fonts | ≤ 3 files, ≤ 300 kB | V3b shipped 19 files / 732 kB | | DOM | ≤ 1500 nodes | Single-file HTML | | Resting `will-change` | 0 elements | Promotion is for motion in flight, not for standing still | | `filter` / `backdrop-filter` on > 50 % of the viewport | 0 | GPU repaint per frame during scroll | **A scrubbed clip has its own line and does not count against the page budget:** ≤ 32 MiB for all desktop clips, ≤ 16 MiB for all mobile clips, fetched as a Blob *after* first paint so it never sits on the LCP path. A clip loaded in the fold breaks both budgets at once. ## 2 · Loading - **Every ``**: `width` and `height` attributes (both — the single largest cause of layout shift), `decoding="async"`, `fetchpriority="high"` on the LCP image, `loading="lazy"` below the fold, `srcset`/`sizes` when it renders under 60 % of the viewport width. - **The hero must be vendored.** Downscale to ~2200 px on the long edge, re-encode WebP, commit it. It must not depend on another company's CDN — measured 2026-09-08, V3b's heaviest resource was a 1.1 MB hero hotlinked from `images.unsplash.com`, which is both a budget failure and a Step 5b rule violation nobody had caught by eye. - **Fonts**: `.woff2` only; `` for the display weight that appears in the fold, and only that one; `font-display: swap`; a metric-matched fallback `@font-face` (`size-adjust`, `ascent-override`, `descent-override`) so the swap costs no shift; one variable file once you need three weights or more; `font-weight` as a property, never `font-variation-settings`; `-webkit-font-smoothing` set once on the root, never per element. - **Iframes**: `loading="lazy"` *and* mounted by an `IntersectionObserver` about one viewport ahead. Three live iframes mounted at load is the heaviest thing a marketing page can do to itself. - **`content-visibility: auto`** with `contain-intrinsic-size` on long sections below the fold. It is the cheapest single win on a twelve-act page. - **preconnect** to any origin the fold actually needs. ## 3 · Rendering - **Animate `transform`, `opacity` and `filter`.** Everything else costs layout or paint per frame. `clip-path` composites only in newer Chromium — treat it as a paint cost elsewhere and keep the animated area small. - **`will-change` only while the element is moving**, removed at rest. Setting it class-wide promotes every match to its own layer for the life of the page, which is itself a jank source on a mid-range GPU. `sc-smooth.js` corrects the engine's own class-level promotions at runtime. - **Blur is expensive in proportion to area.** `backdrop-filter` only on fixed or sticky chrome, never on a full-bleed surface during scroll. Grain film goes on a fixed, `pointer-events: none` pseudo-element at 4–5 % so it is painted once. - **`transition: all` is a defect**, not a shortcut: it animates properties you never meant to animate, including layout-triggering ones, and retargets on every change. - **No layout reads in a scroll handler.** One passive listener that only schedules, one rAF loop that reads and writes, a deadband so the loop stops when nothing moves. The engine's own shape is the model; `window.addEventListener('scroll')` doing `getBoundingClientRect()` per event is the anti-pattern. - **`min-height: 100dvh`, never `height: 100vh`.** The iOS address bar changes `vh` mid-scroll and the act jumps. - **Isolate a continuous animation in a leaf element** so it cannot force its parent to re-render. ## 4 · Motion Timings, easings and the ban list live in [`motion.md`](motion.md); the smoothness rules and the `--sc-ps` contract live in [`motion-smoothness.md`](motion-smoothness.md). The performance-relevant half: - Transitions retarget from their current value; keyframes restart. For anything a user can interrupt, use a transition. - A scrubbed clip needs a **dense GOP** or it seeks like mud — see [`assets.md`](assets.md) § Encoding. A normal web encode places a keyframe every two to five seconds and plays back perfectly while scrubbing terribly. - Stagger at 30–80 ms and cap the number of staggered items; a cascade of forty is forty animations. ## 5 · Measuring ```bash python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/serve.py --port 3000 --root . python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/perf_probe.py --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/page.html --cpu 4 --out shots/perf python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/motion_probe.py --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/page.html \ --track "#hero:--sc-p,#hero:--sc-ps,.plate-card:transform" --out shots/perf ``` Never `python -m http.server`: it is HTTP/1.0 and drops large WebP responses under Chromium on Windows, so you end up measuring a page that failed to load. Both probes are proven in both directions before they are trusted — `tests/perf/{heavy,clean}.html` and `tests/motion/{staircase,smooth}.html`. A check that only ever fires is as useless as one that never does: if a probe flags a known-good reference build, it is over-greedy and gets narrowed, not waived. ## 6 · Never - A hero image on someone else's CDN. - `transition: all`. - `will-change` on a class. - A blurred surface larger than half the viewport, animated during scroll. - More than three font files, or a preload for a weight that is not in the fold. - An iframe mounted at load. - A scroll handler that reads layout. - `height: 100vh` on a full-height act. - Shipping a number from this file that you did not measure on the actual page.

1	# Pace — the third thing people call "not smooth"
2	
3	Damping fixes the value *between* two writes. Pace is the value's own speed, and no
4	amount of damping fixes a speed that changes from act to act. Upstream
5	`worldflight.md` § 7c is the only place in the corpus where someone diagnosed the
6	complaint to root cause, and its first line is the whole problem:
7	
8	> *"Two separate faults get described as 'it doesn't feel smooth', and only one of
9	> them is smoothing."*
10	
11	Read [`../motion-smoothness.md`](../motion-smoothness.md) first — it separates the
12	*stepping* fault (a raw value written 1:1) from the *dropped frames* fault (the page
13	is genuinely slow). This file is the third one, and it is the fault the owner of the
14	`orrery` build actually had.
15	
16	## Inconsistent pace is the worse one
17	
18	```
19	rate = weight / clip_seconds        // hold this within a few percent everywhere
20	```
21	
22	Leg weight divided by clip length is how fast the world moves under the reader's
23	hand. When that number varies from leg to leg, the world surges and drags for no
24	reason the reader can see, and it reads as a fault in the page rather than as pacing.
25	
26	- Every leg with the **same clip length gets the same weight**.
27	- A **longer clip gets a proportional weight** — proportional, not "bigger by feel".
28	
29	Measured upstream on `orrery`: the rate varied by **36 % across ten legs** on the
30	first cut, and the owner's word for it was *"not smooth"*. Evened to a **6 % spread**,
31	the same footage reads as one continuous move. Same clips, same damping, same engine —
32	only the weights changed.
33	
34	That pair is the number to carry: **36 % reads as a defect in the page; 6 % reads as
35	one movement.**
36	
37	## Then slow it down
38	
39	The instinct is to spend as little scroll as possible. A fly-through wants the
40	opposite: the reader is steering a camera, and a camera that answers too eagerly feels
41	twitchy.
42	
43	| | Value |
44	|---|---|
45	| Floor for a world you fly through | **0.21–0.22 vh per second of film** |
46	| What the per-8s line yields | 0.14–0.19 vh/s — *noticeably fast* |
47	| What the per-8s line actually is | a **dead-scroll guardrail, not a taste ceiling** |
48	
49	Exceeding the guardrail is fine and often correct; exceeding it *without checking* is
50	not. The harness defines dead scroll mechanically and will tell you. At 0.216 vh/s a
51	0.12 vh sample gap still advances the clip by half a second — nowhere near dead.
52	
53	## Damping and weights fix different halves
54	
55	> *"The damping is what removes wheel judder; the weights are what remove the
56	> surging."*
57	
58	| Knob | Act page | Worldflight | Why the flight differs |
59	|---|---|---|---|
60	| `data-sc-lerp` | 0.18 (default) | **0.12** | A flight has more legs mounted and more seams than an act page, and the extra damping is what actually removes wheel-event judder |
61	| `data-sc-seam` | 0.12 (default) | **~0.16** | A longer crossfade band gives each join more room to disappear in |
62	
63	`data-sc-lerp` is never 0 and never disabled — a 1:1 playhead reproduces every gap in
64	the wheel event stream as a stutter. (Upstream's hard-rules table attaches a
65	reduced-motion exception to that sentence. It does not port: **F-011** — motion always
66	plays here and no build reads a preference to switch it off.)
67	
68	Neither knob fixes an uneven `rate`. Raising the lerp on a surging flight only makes
69	the surge arrive smoothly — the same way damping a value on a page that cannot hold
70	60 fps makes a smooth curve arrive late.
71	
72	## Changing a weight changes every window
73	
74	Weights are the track. Moving one moves every leg boundary after it, so **every
75	`data-sc-window` has to be recomputed** against the new track and then re-checked on
76	screen. A copy window is tuned to a frame of film, not to a number; redoing the
77	arithmetic is not the same as looking at it.
78	
79	Budget that re-check into any pacing pass. It is the reason pace is settled before the
80	copy windows are, not after.
81	
82	## Measuring it
83	
84	`motion_probe.py` reports `max_step_pct` per tracked value, so an act that surges
85	relative to its neighbours shows up as a spread across runs rather than as a feeling.
86	
87	```bash
88	python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/serve.py --port 3000 --root .
89	python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/motion_probe.py --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/page.html \
90	    --track "#leg1:--sc-ps,#leg2:--sc-ps,#leg3:--sc-ps" --cpu 4 --out shots/motion
91	```
92	
93	Write the per-leg `rate` out as a table from the markup — weight and clip length are
94	both in the source, so this is arithmetic, not a measurement, and there is no excuse
95	for not having it. The spread between the largest and smallest rate is what gate **94**
96	reads.
97	
98	## The bar
99	
100	- Per-leg `rate` spread **≤ 6 %** across the whole flight. 36 % is the measured
101	  failure, not a hypothetical one.
102	- **≥ 0.21 vh per second of film** on anything the reader flies through.
103	- `data-sc-lerp` **0.12** and `data-sc-seam` **~0.16** on a worldflight; the act-page
104	  defaults (0.18 / 0.12) elsewhere.
105	- Every `data-sc-window` re-checked **on screen** after any weight change.
106	- Plus the continuity bar in [`../motion-smoothness.md`](../motion-smoothness.md) §
107	  The bar — `staircase` 0, `max_step_pct` ≤ 3, `frame_p95_ms` ≤ 20 at 4× CPU, zero
108	  frames over 33 ms, both scroll directions.
109	
110	## What the harness cannot tell you
111	
112	`shoot.mjs` waits for the lerp to settle before every shot precisely because *"a
113	screenshot taken mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds, and it makes the
114	run unrepeatable"*. That buys repeatability, not evenness: a contact sheet of settled
115	frames says nothing about the speed between them. Scroll it cold, one word per leg,
116	and diff against the intended curve
117	([`feel-and-fingerprint.md`](feel-and-fingerprint.md) § Peak) before opening
118	`BRIEF.md`.
119	
120	## Related
121	
122	[`../motion-smoothness.md`](../motion-smoothness.md) · [`devices.md`](devices.md) ·
123	[`README.md`](README.md) · [`../performance.md`](../performance.md) · gate **94** ·
124	`scripts/motion_probe.py` · upstream `worldflight.md` §§ 7c, 8, 9 · FEEDBACK.md F-011,
125	F-013.

```

hand. When that number varies from leg to leg, the world surges and drags for no

- A **longer clip gets a proportional weight** — proportional, not "bigger by feel".

Measured upstream on `orrery`: the rate varied by **36 % across ten legs** on the
first cut, and the owner's word for it was *"not smooth"*. Evened to a **6 % spread**,
the same footage reads as one continuous move. Same clips, same damping, same engine —
only the weights changed.

That pair is the number to carry: **36 % reads as a defect in the page; 6 % reads as
one movement.**

## Then slow it down

The instinct is to spend as little scroll as possible. A fly-through wants the
opposite: the reader is steering a camera, and a camera that answers too eagerly feels
twitchy.

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Floor for a world you fly through | **0.21–0.22 vh per second of film** |
| What the per-8s line yields | 0.14–0.19 vh/s — *noticeably fast* |
| What the per-8s line actually is | a **dead-scroll guardrail, not a taste ceiling** |

Exceeding the guardrail is fine and often correct; exceeding it *without checking* is
not. The harness defines dead scroll mechanically and will tell you. At 0.216 vh/s a
0.12 vh sample gap still advances the clip by half a second — nowhere near dead.

## Damping and weights fix different halves

> *"The damping is what removes wheel judder; the weights are what remove the
> surging."*

| Knob | Act page | Worldflight | Why the flight differs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `data-sc-lerp` | 0.18 (default) | **0.12** | A flight has more legs mounted and more seams than an act page, and the extra damping is what actually removes wheel-event judder |
| `data-sc-seam` | 0.12 (default) | **~0.16** | A longer crossfade band gives each join more room to disappear in |

`data-sc-lerp` is never 0 and never disabled — a 1:1 playhead reproduces every gap in
the wheel event stream as a stutter. (Upstream's hard-rules table attaches a
reduced-motion exception to that sentence. It does not port: **F-011** — motion always
plays here and no build reads a preference to switch it off.)

Neither knob fixes an uneven `rate`. Raising the lerp on a surging flight only makes
the surge arrive smoothly — the same way damping a value on a page that cannot hold
60 fps makes a smooth curve arrive late.

## Changing a weight changes every window

Weights are the track. Moving one moves every leg boundary after it, so **every
`data-sc-window` has to be recomputed** against the new track and then re-checked on
screen. A copy window is tuned to a frame of film, not to a number; redoing the
arithmetic is not the same as looking at it.

Budget that re-check into any pacing pass. It is the reason pace is settled before the
copy windows are, not after.

## Measuring it

`motion_probe.py` reports `max_step_pct` per tracked value, so an act that surges
relative to its neighbours shows up as a spread across runs rather than as a feeling.

```bash
python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/serve.py --port 3000 --root .
python ~/.claude/skills/design/scripts/motion_probe.py --url http://127.0.0.1:3000/page.html \
    --track "#leg1:--sc-ps,#leg2:--sc-ps,#leg3:--sc-ps" --cpu 4 --out shots/motion
```

both in the source, so this is arithmetic, not a measurement, and there is no excuse
for not having it. The spread between the largest and smallest rate is what gate **94**
reads.

- Per-leg `rate` spread **≤ 6 %** across the whole flight. 36 % is the measured
  failure, not a hypothetical one.
- **≥ 0.21 vh per second of film** on anything the reader flies through.
- `data-sc-lerp` **0.12** and `data-sc-seam` **~0.16** on a worldflight; the act-page
  defaults (0.18 / 0.12) elsewhere.
- Every `data-sc-window` re-checked **on screen** after any weight change.
- Plus the continuity bar in [`../motion-smoothness.md`](../motion-smoothness.md) §
  The bar — `staircase` 0, `max_step_pct` ≤ 3, `frame_p95_ms` ≤ 20 at 4× CPU, zero
  frames over 33 ms, both scroll directions.

## What the harness cannot tell you

`shoot.mjs` waits for the lerp to settle before every shot precisely because *"a
screenshot taken mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds, and it makes the

and diff against the intended curve
([`feel-and-fingerprint.md`](feel-and-fingerprint.md) § Peak) before opening
`BRIEF.md`.

## Related

[`../motion-smoothness.md`](../motion-smoothness.md) · [`devices.md`](devices.md) ·
[`README.md`](README.md) · [`../performance.md`](../performance.md) · gate **94** ·

1	# The lift — what replaces "just run polish"
2	
3	`impeccable polish` is a *last* pass and says so: it "preserves the incumbent visual
4	world" and "does not add animation merely to make polish visible". Pointed at a whole
5	page that is merely competent, it returns a slightly tidier competent page. Every other
6	impeccable command ends by handing off to polish; polish is the handoff target, not the
7	procedure.
8	
9	The lift is the procedure. Each pass is a named skill invocation, in an order the
10	upstream references themselves prescribe, with a mechanical gate between passes.
11	
12	## The sequence
13	
14	| # | Pass | Invocation | Output |
15	|---|---|---|---|
16	| 1 | Read-only review | [`verbs/review.md`](verbs/review.md) — slop audit + `Skill(a11y-audit)` + [`verbs/critique.md`](verbs/critique.md) + `Skill(review-animations)` | One ranked table, ≤ 15 rows, Block or Approve |
17	| 2 | The quartet, in parallel | `design-critic`, `design-heuristics`, `design-a11y-reviewer`, `design-perf-reviewer` | Four reports on the shared contract below |
18	| 3 | Where motion belongs | `Skill(find-animation-opportunities)` + `Skill(animation-vocabulary)` | ≤ 5 proposals with exact values **and a Rejected list** |
19	| 4 | Fix plans | `improve-animations`' PLAN-TEMPLATE per finding | `plans/NNN-slug.md`: Problem / Target / Conventions / Steps / Boundaries / Verification incl. a feel-check |
20	| 5 | Fix passes, one per round | (a) `impeccable layout` → (b) `impeccable typeset` → (c) `impeccable colorize` *only if* the critique says flat or grey → (d) `Skill(animate)` + `Skill(emil-design-eng)` → (e) `impeccable delight` *only if* the brief carries a delight thesis → (f) the copy gate → (g) `impeccable harden` → (h) `impeccable optimize` against the probe reports → (i) `impeccable polish` **last** | One commit per pass, screenshots after each |
21	| 6 | Mechanical gate after every pass | `detect.mjs --json`, `preflight_taste.py`, `scroll_verify.py`, `perf_probe.py`, `motion_probe.py`, `contrast_over_media.py` | All green before the next pass |
22	| 7 | Round again | Back to 1 | Stop when a whole pass finds nothing material **and the critic writes "beats" for each locked reference** |
23	
24	Cap: six rounds per cell. Then stop and hand Anton a table of what is still open, rather
25	than iterating quietly forever.
26	
27	## Triage order inside a round
28	
29	From `impeccable/reference/polish.md`: **broken → states → flow and hierarchy → visual →
30	code.** A colour decision taken before a broken state is fixed is a decision taken about
31	the wrong page. Within "visual", most material first: a fix that changes what the page
32	*is* outranks one that changes how it is finished.
33	
34	## The reviewer contract
35	
36	All four reviewers return the same shape, borrowed from impeccable's finish-reviewer:
37	
38	1. First line, one disposition word: `recapture` · `rebuild` · `fix` · `ship`.
39	2. Then exactly five sections:
40	   - **persistence** — did the previous round's fixes survive?
41	   - **fidelity** — against the target picture, screen by screen (F-007).
42	   - **ceiling** — what each locked reference still does better, one line per reference.
43	   - **material_fixes** — at most 8, most material first, each with a target value or a
44	     reference image, never "make it nicer".
45	   - **keep** — what must not be touched.
46	
47	The critic's ceiling section carries the honest sentence **per locked reference**:
48	"beats garden-eight on X, loses to mattis-studio on Y". A single lump verdict hides which
49	reference is actually beating you.
50	
51	Reconciliation when they disagree: **accessibility > performance > usability > brief >
52	personas > escalate**. Performance sits above usability because a page that drops frames
53	cannot be judged on usability at all.
54	
55	Every finding is verified against the pixels by whoever merges the reports. A reviewer
56	report is a claim, not a fact.
57	
58	## When a pass is skipped
59	
60	`bolder`, `quieter` and `distill` run **only** when pass 1 or 2 says a named section is
61	flat, loud or overloaded. `colorize` runs only on a flatness finding. `delight` runs only
62	when the brief declares a delight thesis. Skipping is the default; running one without a
63	finding behind it is how a page drifts away from its own direction.
64	
65	## Not part of the lift
66	
67	- `impeccable live` — needs a dev server and an overlay; it is Anton's own manual
68	  iteration after delivery, not a chain step.
69	- `impeccable onboard` / `extract` — Operate surfaces and design-system maintenance.
70	- `impeccable document` — runs *after* ship, from the built code, never before.
71	- `prototype` — the bake-off already has `board.py`.
72	- The gstack quartet (`design-review`, `design-shotgun`, `design-html`,
73	  `design-consultation`) — a parallel pipeline. Pick one lane per project; what is worth
74	  borrowing from it is already ported into `verbs/review.md`.
75	
76	## Stopping
77	
78	Two conditions, both required: a full pass 1–2 that finds nothing material, and the
79	critic writing "beats" for every locked reference. "Stands up beside them" is not the
80	bar. If you cannot say it yet, the page is not finished — and if you have said it six
81	times without it becoming true, the concept is what needs changing, not the polish.
82

the wrong page. Within "visual", most material first: a fix that changes what the page
*is* outranks one that changes how it is finished.

## The reviewer contract

All four reviewers return the same shape, borrowed from impeccable's finish-reviewer:

1. First line, one disposition word: `recapture` · `rebuild` · `fix` · `ship`.
2. Then exactly five sections:
   - **persistence** — did the previous round's fixes survive?
   - **fidelity** — against the target picture, screen by screen (F-007).
   - **ceiling** — what each locked reference still does better, one line per reference.
   - **material_fixes** — at most 8, most material first, each with a target value or a
     reference image, never "make it nicer".
   - **keep** — what must not be touched.

The critic's ceiling section carries the honest sentence **per locked reference**:
"beats garden-eight on X, loses to mattis-studio on Y". A single lump verdict hides which
reference is actually beating you.

Reconciliation when they disagree: **accessibility > performance > usability > brief >
personas > escalate**. Performance sits above usability because a page that drops frames
cannot be judged on usability at all.

Every finding is verified against the pixels by whoever merges the reports. A reviewer
report is a claim, not a fact.

## When a pass is skipped

`bolder`, `quieter` and `distill` run **only** when pass 1 or 2 says a named section is
flat, loud or overloaded. `colorize` runs only on a flatness finding. `delight` runs only
when the brief declares a delight thesis. Skipping is the default; running one without a
finding behind it is how a page drifts away from its own direction.

## Not part of the lift

- `impeccable live` — needs a dev server and an overlay; it is Anton's own manual
  iteration after delivery, not a chain step.
- `impeccable onboard` / `extract` — Operate surfaces and design-system maintenance.
- `impeccable document` — runs *after* ship, from the built code, never before.
- `prototype` — the bake-off already has `board.py`.
- The gstack quartet (`design-review`, `design-shotgun`, `design-html`,
  `design-consultation`) — a parallel pipeline. Pick one lane per project; what is worth
  borrowing from it is already ported into `verbs/review.md`.

## Stopping

Two conditions, both required: a full pass 1–2 that finds nothing material, and the
critic writing "beats" for every locked reference. "Stands up beside them" is not the
bar. If you cannot say it yet, the page is not finished — and if you have said it six
times without it becoming true, the concept is what needs changing, not the polish.

36	## 2. Direct manipulation — 1:1 tracking
37	
38	> "Touch and content should move together."
39	
40	When the user drags something, it must stay glued to the finger — and respect the offset from *where they grabbed it*. Snapping to the element's center on grab breaks the illusion immediately.
41	
42	- Use Pointer Events with `setPointerCapture` so tracking continues even when the pointer leaves the element's bounds.
43	- Track a short **velocity/position history** (last few `pointermove` events), not just the current point — you'll need velocity at release.
44	
45	```js
46	el.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
47	  el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
48	  const grabOffset = e.clientY - el.getBoundingClientRect().top; // respect where they grabbed
49	  // ...track position + timestamp history for velocity
50	});
51	```
52	
53	## 3. Interruptibility — the single most important principle
54	
55	> "The thought and the gesture happen in parallel."
56	
57	Every animation must be interruptible and redirectable at any moment. A user must be able to grab a moving element mid-flight and reverse it without waiting for the animation to finish. A closing modal the user grabs again should follow the finger — not finish closing first, then reopen.
58	
59	- **Never lock out input during a transition.**
60	- **Always animate from the *presentation* (current) value, never the target value.** On interrupt, read the element's live on-screen transform and start the new animation from there. Starting from the logical/target value causes a visible jump.
61	- **Avoid CSS transitions and `@keyframes` for anything gesture-driven** — they can't be smoothly grabbed and reversed mid-flight. Springs animate from the current value by default, which is exactly what interruption needs.
62	- **When a gesture reverses, blend velocity — don't hard-cut it.** Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a "brick wall." Spring libraries that carry velocity through a re-target avoid it. (This is what iOS's *additive animations* do natively; on the web, choose a spring library that re-targets from the current velocity.)
63	- **Decompose 2D motion into independent X and Y springs.** A single spring on a 2D distance desyncs when X and Y have different velocities.
64	
65	## 4. Behavior over animation — use springs
66	
67	> "Think of animation as a conversation between you and the object, not something prescribed by the interface."
68	
69	A pre-scripted, fixed-duration animation can't respond to new input. A spring can — new input just changes the target, and the motion stays continuous. Reach for springs for anything a user can touch.
70	
71	Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet (mass/stiffness/damping) with two designer-friendly parameters. Think in these:
72	
73	- **Damping ratio** — controls overshoot. `1.0` = critically damped, no bounce, smooth settle. `< 1.0` = overshoots and oscillates. Lower = bouncier.
74	- **Response** — how quickly the value reaches the target, in seconds. Lower = snappier. **This is not "duration"** — a spring has no fixed duration; its settle time emerges from the parameters.
75	
76	**Defaults:**
77	- Start most UI at **damping `1.0`** (critically damped) — graceful and non-distracting.
78	- Add bounce (**damping ~`0.8`**) **only when the gesture itself carried momentum** (a flick, a throw, a drag release). Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right.
79	
80	**Concrete values Apple ships:**
81	
82	| Interaction | Damping | Response |
83	| --- | --- | --- |
84	| Move / reposition (e.g. PiP) | `1.0` | `0.4` |
85	| Rotation | `0.8` | `0.4` |
86	| Drawer / sheet | `0.8` | `0.3` |
87	
88	**Web mapping (Motion / Framer Motion):** the `bounce` + `duration` spring API maps closely to Apple's damping + response. A safe house style is `damping: 1.0` springs everywhere by default; reserve bounce for momentum-driven, physical interactions.
89	
90	```js
91	import { animate } from 'motion';
92	
93	// Critically damped default (no overshoot)
94	animate(el, { y: 0 }, { type: 'spring', bounce: 0, duration: 0.4 });
95	
96	// Momentum interaction — a little bounce, only because a flick preceded it
97	animate(el, { y: target }, { type: 'spring', bounce: 0.2, duration: 0.4 });
98	```
99	
100	## 5. Velocity handoff — the seam between drag and animation
101	
102	When a gesture ends, the animation must **continue at the finger's exact velocity**, so there's no visible seam between dragging and animating. This is the detail that most separates "fluid" from "fine."
103	
104	Pass the pointer's release velocity as the spring's initial velocity. Some spring APIs want **relative** velocity — normalize it by the remaining distance to the target:
105	
106	```
107	relativeVelocity = gestureVelocity / (targetValue − currentValue)
108	```
109	
110	Example: element at `y=50`, target `y=150` (100px to go), finger moving 50px/s → initial spring velocity = `50 / 100 = 0.5`. Framer Motion / Motion take absolute px/s velocity directly (`velocity` option), so you usually hand it the raw value.
111	
112	## 6. Momentum projection — animate to where the gesture is *going*
113	
114	> "Take a small input and make a big output."
115	
116	Don't snap to the nearest boundary from the *release point*. Use velocity to **project the resting position** — exactly like scroll deceleration — then snap to the target nearest that projected point. This is what makes a flick feel like it throws the element.
117	
118	Apple's exact projection function (from the *Designing Fluid Interfaces* sample code):
119	
120	```js
121	// decelerationRate ≈ 0.998 for normal scroll feel; 0.99 for snappier
122	function project(initialVelocity /* px/s */, decelerationRate = 0.998) {
123	  return (initialVelocity / 1000) * decelerationRate / (1 - decelerationRate);
124	}
125	
126	const projectedEndpoint = currentPosition + project(releaseVelocity);
127	const target = nearestSnapPoint(projectedEndpoint);   // choose target from the projection
128	animateSpringTo(target, { velocity: releaseVelocity }); // then hand off velocity (§5)
129	```
130	
131	Note: the physics-textbook `v²/(2·decel)` is *not* what Apple ships — use the exponential-decay form above. This is the standard behavior in good bottom-sheets and carousels (Vaul, Embla).
132	
133	## 7. Spatial consistency — symmetric paths, anchored origins
134	
135	> "If something disappears one way, we expect it to emerge from where it came."
136	
137	- **Enter and exit along the same path.** A panel that slides in from the right must dismiss to the right. In-from-right / out-the-bottom feels disconnected and confusing.
138	- **Anchor interactions to their source.** A menu, popover, or sheet should originate from the element that triggered it — set `transform-origin` to the trigger, so the spatial relationship between button and content is obvious. (This is the same origin-awareness point as popovers scaling from their trigger, not their center.)
139	- **Mirror the easing on reversible transitions** so the outbound path matches the return path (use inverse cubic-bézier control points for the two directions).
140	
141	## 8. Hint in the direction of the gesture
142	
143	Humans predict a final state from a trajectory. Intermediate motion should telegraph where things are going — Control Center modules "grow up and out toward your finger." Make the in-between frames point at the outcome, not just interpolate blindly to it.
144	
145	## 9. Rubber-banding — soft boundaries
146	
147	At an edge, resist progressively instead of stopping hard. A hard stop reads as "frozen"; continuous resistance reads as "responsive, but there's nothing more here." Apply damping that increases the further past the boundary the user drags.
148	
149	```js
150	// The further past the bound, the less the element follows — real things slow before they stop
151	function rubberband(overshoot, dimension, constant = 0.55) {
152	  return (overshoot * dimension * constant) / (dimension + constant * Math.abs(overshoot));
153	}
154	```
155	
156	## 10. Gesture design details (the "feel" checklist)
157	
158	- **Tap:** highlight on touch-*down* (instant), commit on touch-*up*. Add ~10px of hysteresis/hit padding around the target, and allow cancel-by-dragging-away and back.
159	- **Drag/swipe:** require a small movement threshold (hysteresis, ~10px) before committing to a direction, then track 1:1.
160	- **Detect all plausible gestures in parallel from the first move**, then confidently cancel the losers once intent is clear. Avoid recognizers that only report a *final* state (`swipeleft`-type events) — they throw away the continuous tracking you need for feedback.
161	- **Minimize disambiguation delays.** Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps; only pay that cost where double-tap truly exists.
162	
163	## 11. Frame-level smoothness
164	
165	Smoothness is about *what's in the frames*, not just the frame rate.
166	
167	- Keep the per-frame positional change below the perception threshold to avoid strobing.
168	- For very fast motion, a subtle **motion blur / stretch** encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak.
169	- `requestAnimationFrame` is the web's display-synced clock (Apple uses `CADisplayLink`). Animate only compositor-friendly properties — `transform` and `opacity` — and hint with `will-change` where motion is imminent.

## 2. Direct manipulation — 1:1 tracking

> "Touch and content should move together."

When the user drags something, it must stay glued to the finger — and respect the offset from *where they grabbed it*. Snapping to the element's center on grab breaks the illusion immediately.

- Use Pointer Events with `setPointerCapture` so tracking continues even when the pointer leaves the element's bounds.
- Track a short **velocity/position history** (last few `pointermove` events), not just the current point — you'll need velocity at release.

```js
el.addEventListener('pointerdown', (e) => {
  el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
  const grabOffset = e.clientY - el.getBoundingClientRect().top; // respect where they grabbed
  // ...track position + timestamp history for velocity
});
```

## 3. Interruptibility — the single most important principle

> "The thought and the gesture happen in parallel."

Every animation must be interruptible and redirectable at any moment. A user must be able to grab a moving element mid-flight and reverse it without waiting for the animation to finish. A closing modal the user grabs again should follow the finger — not finish closing first, then reopen.

- **Never lock out input during a transition.**
- **Always animate from the *presentation* (current) value, never the target value.** On interrupt, read the element's live on-screen transform and start the new animation from there. Starting from the logical/target value causes a visible jump.
- **Avoid CSS transitions and `@keyframes` for anything gesture-driven** — they can't be smoothly grabbed and reversed mid-flight. Springs animate from the current value by default, which is exactly what interruption needs.
- **When a gesture reverses, blend velocity — don't hard-cut it.** Replacing one animation with another at a reversal creates a velocity discontinuity, a "brick wall." Spring libraries that carry velocity through a re-target avoid it. (This is what iOS's *additive animations* do natively; on the web, choose a spring library that re-targets from the current velocity.)
- **Decompose 2D motion into independent X and Y springs.** A single spring on a 2D distance desyncs when X and Y have different velocities.

## 4. Behavior over animation — use springs

> "Think of animation as a conversation between you and the object, not something prescribed by the interface."

A pre-scripted, fixed-duration animation can't respond to new input. A spring can — new input just changes the target, and the motion stays continuous. Reach for springs for anything a user can touch.

Apple deliberately replaced the physics triplet (mass/stiffness/damping) with two designer-friendly parameters. Think in these:

- **Damping ratio** — controls overshoot. `1.0` = critically damped, no bounce, smooth settle. `< 1.0` = overshoots and oscillates. Lower = bouncier.
- **Response** — how quickly the value reaches the target, in seconds. Lower = snappier. **This is not "duration"** — a spring has no fixed duration; its settle time emerges from the parameters.

**Defaults:**
- Start most UI at **damping `1.0`** (critically damped) — graceful and non-distracting.
- Add bounce (**damping ~`0.8`**) **only when the gesture itself carried momentum** (a flick, a throw, a drag release). Overshoot on a menu that just faded in feels wrong; overshoot on a card you flicked feels right.

**Concrete values Apple ships:**

| Interaction | Damping | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Move / reposition (e.g. PiP) | `1.0` | `0.4` |
| Rotation | `0.8` | `0.4` |
| Drawer / sheet | `0.8` | `0.3` |

**Web mapping (Motion / Framer Motion):** the `bounce` + `duration` spring API maps closely to Apple's damping + response. A safe house style is `damping: 1.0` springs everywhere by default; reserve bounce for momentum-driven, physical interactions.

```js
import { animate } from 'motion';

// Critically damped default (no overshoot)
animate(el, { y: 0 }, { type: 'spring', bounce: 0, duration: 0.4 });

// Momentum interaction — a little bounce, only because a flick preceded it
animate(el, { y: target }, { type: 'spring', bounce: 0.2, duration: 0.4 });
```

## 5. Velocity handoff — the seam between drag and animation

When a gesture ends, the animation must **continue at the finger's exact velocity**, so there's no visible seam between dragging and animating. This is the detail that most separates "fluid" from "fine."

Pass the pointer's release velocity as the spring's initial velocity. Some spring APIs want **relative** velocity — normalize it by the remaining distance to the target:

```
relativeVelocity = gestureVelocity / (targetValue − currentValue)
```

Example: element at `y=50`, target `y=150` (100px to go), finger moving 50px/s → initial spring velocity = `50 / 100 = 0.5`. Framer Motion / Motion take absolute px/s velocity directly (`velocity` option), so you usually hand it the raw value.

## 6. Momentum projection — animate to where the gesture is *going*

> "Take a small input and make a big output."

Don't snap to the nearest boundary from the *release point*. Use velocity to **project the resting position** — exactly like scroll deceleration — then snap to the target nearest that projected point. This is what makes a flick feel like it throws the element.

Apple's exact projection function (from the *Designing Fluid Interfaces* sample code):

```js
// decelerationRate ≈ 0.998 for normal scroll feel; 0.99 for snappier
function project(initialVelocity /* px/s */, decelerationRate = 0.998) {
  return (initialVelocity / 1000) * decelerationRate / (1 - decelerationRate);
}

const projectedEndpoint = currentPosition + project(releaseVelocity);
const target = nearestSnapPoint(projectedEndpoint);   // choose target from the projection
animateSpringTo(target, { velocity: releaseVelocity }); // then hand off velocity (§5)
```

Note: the physics-textbook `v²/(2·decel)` is *not* what Apple ships — use the exponential-decay form above. This is the standard behavior in good bottom-sheets and carousels (Vaul, Embla).

## 7. Spatial consistency — symmetric paths, anchored origins

> "If something disappears one way, we expect it to emerge from where it came."

- **Enter and exit along the same path.** A panel that slides in from the right must dismiss to the right. In-from-right / out-the-bottom feels disconnected and confusing.
- **Anchor interactions to their source.** A menu, popover, or sheet should originate from the element that triggered it — set `transform-origin` to the trigger, so the spatial relationship between button and content is obvious. (This is the same origin-awareness point as popovers scaling from their trigger, not their center.)
- **Mirror the easing on reversible transitions** so the outbound path matches the return path (use inverse cubic-bézier control points for the two directions).

## 8. Hint in the direction of the gesture

Humans predict a final state from a trajectory. Intermediate motion should telegraph where things are going — Control Center modules "grow up and out toward your finger." Make the in-between frames point at the outcome, not just interpolate blindly to it.

## 9. Rubber-banding — soft boundaries

At an edge, resist progressively instead of stopping hard. A hard stop reads as "frozen"; continuous resistance reads as "responsive, but there's nothing more here." Apply damping that increases the further past the boundary the user drags.

```js
// The further past the bound, the less the element follows — real things slow before they stop
function rubberband(overshoot, dimension, constant = 0.55) {
  return (overshoot * dimension * constant) / (dimension + constant * Math.abs(overshoot));
}
```

## 10. Gesture design details (the "feel" checklist)

- **Tap:** highlight on touch-*down* (instant), commit on touch-*up*. Add ~10px of hysteresis/hit padding around the target, and allow cancel-by-dragging-away and back.
- **Drag/swipe:** require a small movement threshold (hysteresis, ~10px) before committing to a direction, then track 1:1.
- **Detect all plausible gestures in parallel from the first move**, then confidently cancel the losers once intent is clear. Avoid recognizers that only report a *final* state (`swipeleft`-type events) — they throw away the continuous tracking you need for feedback.
- **Minimize disambiguation delays.** Double-tap detection unavoidably delays single taps; only pay that cost where double-tap truly exists.

## 11. Frame-level smoothness

Smoothness is about *what's in the frames*, not just the frame rate.

- Keep the per-frame positional change below the perception threshold to avoid strobing.
- For very fast motion, a subtle **motion blur / stretch** encodes speed and reads better than a hard sharp streak.
- `requestAnimationFrame` is the web's display-synced clock (Apple uses `CADisplayLink`). Animate only compositor-friendly properties — `transform` and `opacity` — and hint with `will-change` where motion is imminent.

112	B-K1-nogate, r7 B-K1) on top of two seed rows, and typographic poster has five (r1 K3, r2
113	R6, r6 A-K2 and B-K2, r7 B-K2). Continuous world is a five-row family (M1, V1, V2, V3,
114	V3b) that also shares nav treatment and close pattern by construction, because every r5
115	variant inherited M1's chrome and its two closing objects; those five rows clear the gate

118	nowhere left to differ.

121	scrolling top row with wordmark and contact (M1, V1, V2, V3, V3b) and the fixed minimal
122	bar with logo left and contact right that darkens or lightens per ground (r6 A-K1, B-K1,

124	with a light-serif headline in the water (four rows) and the crushed poster wordmark with
125	the example screenshots showing through or beside the letters (four rows). The r7 rows
126	record their own shared dimensions honestly — each clears the gate at exactly 4 of 6
127	against its r6 predecessor, with grammar and nav knowingly shared — so a v3 of either
128	concept cannot reuse the hero device, the act shape or the close as well.
129

131	R5, the r3 build, r4 M1 and M2, and r5 V1, V2, V3 and V3b. Those cells' own files name
132	grammar, world and palette but never a register from the six-name vocabulary, and no
133	sibling file names it for them either. On 2026-09-09 the column was filled for all ten by
134	reading each cell's `index.html` directly (and, for the r3 build and r4 M2, its 1440 fold
135	as pixels) against `design/SKILL.md`'s register table and its "what varies with register"
136	markers: face, grain, buttons versus typeset links, ground and subject. Every one of the
137	ten reads as **modern clean** — one lineage, sans display with mono as register only, no
138	serif and no grain anywhere, one blue accent, ledgers over cards, and a precision subject
139	— which is the same read the registry already recorded for r1 K1, K2, K5, K6 and r2 R1
140	and R2. Each cell states the file it was derived from, so the derivation is auditable and
141	declared as post-hoc, exactly like the seven seed rows above.

# Design fingerprint registry

The fingerprint gate for scroll-choreographed Persuade/Experience builds. See
`.agents/skills/design/references/scroll/feel-and-fingerprint.md` § The
fingerprint gate for the rule: **a new build must differ from EVERY existing
row on at least 4 of the 6 dimension columns**, checked row by row, not
averaged across the table. If a planned build fails the gate, change the
plan, not this file — rewriting a row to make a new build fit is the one
thing that makes this registry worthless.

Seeded 2026-09-03 with one row per existing example site in
`anti-slop-design/sites/`. These sites predate scroll-craft integration and
were not built against the nine-device kit or the eight named grammars — the
Grammar, Signature move and Register columns below are an honest read of what
each page actually does, mapped onto scroll-craft's vocabulary after the
fact, not a claim that they were built to it. Where a site has no bespoke
interaction beyond an ordinary reveal-on-scroll, the Signature move column
says `none` — that is a finding, not a gap in the audit.

| Build | Grammar | Nav treatment | Hero device | Act-sequence shape | Close pattern | Signature move | Register | World / palette | Path |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

No photography | ~7 sections: nav > hero > logo bar (6 fake wordmarks) > 3-icon feature-card grid > 4-stat metric grid > centred CTA > one-line footer | Plain centred CTA (heading/subhead/single pill button) trailing into a generic one-line copyright footer — trails off, no address or distinct voice | none — no bespoke interaction at all, not even a scroll reveal; static Tailwind hover states only | none of the six — generic gradient-on-white SaaS look, the anti-register the others are defined against | Inter; bg #FBFAF7, text #1F2937, gradient #6366F1→#8B5CF6→#EC4899, slate grays | `anti-slop-design/sites/before-ai-slop.html` |

## Reading this table before a new build

Three grammar collisions already exist among these seven rows: Calyx,
Hyperborea and Vintergatan all read as chaptered editorial, and Vinterspelen
leans the same way with a gallery inflection. A new chaptered-editorial build
has to clear 3 more dimensions against **each** of those four rows
individually — nav treatment and hero device are the two that repeat across
them most (folio/edition-strip nav, type-in-photo or split-poster heroes), so
those are the columns most likely to collide again. Hōrai and Tidvatten share
grammar (filmic one-shot), a fixed minimal bar, a JS-parallax full-bleed
hero, and a bell-curve-scrub pinned set-piece as their signature move's
underlying mechanism — a third filmic one-shot build with a scrub-driven
pinned set-piece would need a genuinely different mechanism for the move, not
just different numbers on screen, to clear dimension 6 meaningfully even
though the gate counts it as free.

`before-ai-slop.html` is not a build to avoid colliding with — it is the
negative reference. Any real build should differ from it on every dimension
by construction.

## Alunix concept builds, rounds 1–7 (appended 2026-09-09)

Twenty-nine rows, one per built `index.html` under `anti-slop-design/tests/alunix-*`.
Every column is derived from the cell's own files: the built HTML (nav markup, section
list, `data-sc-act` attributes, `:root` custom properties, font links), its `NOTES.md`
or `BRIEF.md`, and its desktop fold screenshot read as an image. Where a cell's own
files carry no evidence for a column, the cell says `?` rather than a guess — that is a
finding about the cell's documentation, not a licence to treat the dimension as free.

Duplicates were excluded, not counted twice: `alunix-ab-r6/board/cells/*` are byte-identical
copies of the seven r6 runs, `alunix-ab-r7/board/cells/K1-1` and `K2-1` are byte-identical

Rounds 1–2 and 6 predate scroll-craft integration in those cells (no `data-sc-*` in the
markup); their act shapes are hand-rolled. Rounds 3–5 and 7 run the engine. In r6 and r7,
arm A is the Claude-native control (Anthropic's `frontend-design` system prompt, no skills,
no hooks) and arm B is this chain; `B-K1-nogate` is the r6 chain run where the gate never

### What these rows share, and what the next Alunix build has to avoid

Grammar has been spent hard. Chaptered editorial now has five rows here (r1 K4, r2 R2, R3,
R4, r4 M2) on top of the four seed rows, filmic one-shot has four (r6 A-K1, B-K1,
B-K1-nogate, r7 B-K1) on top of two seed rows, and typographic poster has five (r1 K3, r2
R6, r6 A-K2 and B-K2, r7 B-K2). Continuous world is a five-row family (M1, V1, V2, V3,
V3b) that also shares nav treatment and close pattern by construction, because every r5
variant inherited M1's chrome and its two closing objects; those five rows clear the gate
against each other only on hero device, act shape and signature move, which is exactly 3
of the 5 non-free dimensions, the bare minimum. A sixth build in that family would have
nowhere left to differ.

Two nav patterns repeat across rounds and should be treated as used up: the thin
scrolling top row with wordmark and contact (M1, V1, V2, V3, V3b) and the fixed minimal
bar with logo left and contact right that darkens or lightens per ground (r6 A-K1, B-K1,
B-K1-nogate, r7 B-K1). Two hero devices likewise: the full-bleed blue-hour photograph
with a light-serif headline in the water (four rows) and the crushed poster wordmark with
the example screenshots showing through or beside the letters (four rows). The r7 rows
record their own shared dimensions honestly — each clears the gate at exactly 4 of 6
against its r6 predecessor, with grammar and nav knowingly shared — so a v3 of either
concept cannot reuse the hero device, the act shape or the close as well.

Ten rows carried `?` in Register when the r1–r7 block was first appended: r2 R3, R4 and
R5, the r3 build, r4 M1 and M2, and r5 V1, V2, V3 and V3b. Those cells' own files name
grammar, world and palette but never a register from the six-name vocabulary, and no
sibling file names it for them either. On 2026-09-09 the column was filled for all ten by
reading each cell's `index.html` directly (and, for the r3 build and r4 M2, its 1440 fold
as pixels) against `design/SKILL.md`'s register table and its "what varies with register"
markers: face, grain, buttons versus typeset links, ground and subject. Every one of the
ten reads as **modern clean** — one lineage, sans display with mono as register only, no
serif and no grain anywhere, one blue accent, ledgers over cards, and a precision subject
— which is the same read the registry already recorded for r1 K1, K2, K5, K6 and r2 R1
and R2. Each cell states the file it was derived from, so the derivation is auditable and
declared as post-hoc, exactly like the seven seed rows above.

Ett nytt koncept får avvika helt från det.

## Evidence on Hand

Detta är hela beviskassan. Inget annat får synas på sidan.

**Tre exempelsajter, live i `<iframe>`, med sina låsta bildtexter:**

| Sajt | Fil | Rad att använda |
|---|---|---|
| Calyx | `/sites/calyx.html` | `Exempelsida: Calyx, florist i Stockholm` |
| Hōrai | `/sites/horai.html` | `Exempelsida: Hōrai, Asian fusion-koncept` |
| Hyperborea | `/sites/hyperborea.html` | `Exempelsida: Hyperborea, konferens i Lund` |

De tre exempelsajterna är de enda kunder som får synas.

**Skärmbilder av dem:** `assets/demo-calyx.webp`, `assets/demo-horai.webp`,
`assets/demo-hyperborea.webp`.

**Tre paket med pris:** `26 900 kr`, `38 900 kr`, `Pris vid förfrågan`, med paketraderna
ordagrant som de står under Capabilities and Constraints.

**En adress:** `kontakt@alunix.se`, som text och som mailto.

**Logotypfiler:** `assets/logo-white.svg`, `assets/logo-black.svg`.

**Ordagrann copy:** hela listan under Brand Commitments.

## Absences Future Work Must Not Fabricate

Inget av det här finns i beviskassan. Det får därför aldrig uppstå i en design, en bildtext,
en platshållare eller en bildprompt:

- Kunder utöver de tre exempelsajterna.
- Omdömen, recensioner och "nöjda kunder".
- Citat från någon utanför sidan.
- Logotypväggar.
- Stjärnor och betyg.
- Ett team att visa upp. Personer, porträtt, namn, roller.
- Ett kontor att visa upp. Inga foton som läses som "vårt kontor" eller "vårt team".
- Antal år i branschen.
- Antal projekt, antal kunder, antal leveranser.
- Påhittade tal överhuvudtaget. De enda siffrorna vi har är `26 900 kr` och `38 900 kr`, och
  tjänsternas numrering 01 till 03.
- Namnet Klova. Det får aldrig förekomma.

## Product Principles

1. **Beviset ska gå att använda, inte bara ses.** De tre sajterna är riktiga och körs live på
   sidan. Ramar som visats förblir användbara.
2. **Varje siffra på sidan är en siffra vi kan stå för.** Vi har två priser och en numrering.
   Fler tal finns inte, så fler tal skrivs inte.
3. **Priset står framme.** Två paket har ett utskrivet pris. Det tredje säger `Pris vid
   förfrågan` och inget annat.
4. **En adress, inget formulär.** `kontakt@alunix.se` är hela kontaktvägen, som text och som
   mailto.
5. **Vi talar i vi-form och kort.** Fakta före adjektiv. Aldrig "jag".

464	| "h1 48 / h2 32"-skala | **Frånvarande.** Skalan är ≥ 5× enligt TASTE § 2.4: display ~112 px (avslutsrubriken och liggarens tal) mot brödtext 15 px; mellannivån 32 px existerar inte, mellanrubriker är monoetiketter i 11 px med tracking. |
465	| Dekorativa blobbar | **Frånvarande.** Den enda formen i K4:s lager utöver typ är delarens hårlinje, och den är sidans nav. Inget ritas som dekoration. |
466	| Tre lika feature-kort | **Frånvarande.** Tre tjänster = tre rader i olika längd; tre paket = en stycklista med ledarpunkter. Aldrig tre lådor bredvid varandra, aldrig "populärast". |
467	| **F-006** — glaskort, dashboard-över-foto, "live"-punkter, telemetri-chrome | **Frånvarande i K4:s lager, och detta är den känsligaste punkten i cellen.** Antagonisten *innehåller* ett div-byggt dashboardkort. K4 får därför aldrig visa ett eget tal om delarens läge, aldrig en procentavläsning, aldrig en statuschip, aldrig en live-prick, aldrig en etikett som säger vilket läge sidan är i. **Kontrollen i R2/R3:** varje element i K4:s eget lager ska kunna namnges som *rubrik*, *monoetikett*, *liggarrad*, *hårlinje* eller *delare*. Kan det inte det ska det bort. |
468	| **Gate 47** — omritat chrome (webbläsarfält, telefonram) | **Frånvarande.** De två sajterna monteras som `<iframe>` utan ritad webbläsarram, utan flikrad, utan URL-fält, utan trafikljusprickar och utan telefonbezel. Delaren är en linje mellan två ytor, inte en ram runt någon av dem. `paper`-postens produktfönster med trafikljusprickar är uttryckligen lämnat. |

Skillnadsliggaren är typografi, inte en graf, inte en sparkline, inte ett stapeldiagram — `mode`s statkort och `customer-io`s chattpanel är båda avvisade av det skälet. |

Träffytan är 44 px bred och osynlig, och `cursor: col-resize` är hela affordansen (gate 88 + `apple-design` § fine pointer). (c) **Den återgår aldrig till mitten.** En slider är en leksak som nollställer sig; K4:s delare har ett mål som ägs av scrollpositionen, och ett släpp lämnas vidare till det målet, inte till 50 %. # Alunix r8 — målbildsgrind, cell K4

Skriven av arkitekten 2026-09-09/10. Denna fil äger **bara** K4. Lead slår ihop V3c, K3 och
K4 till `concepts.md`; den här filen skrivs aldrig in i den av mig.

Målbilden är `tests/alunix-r8/malbilder/K4.md` (planens § 7.5, ordagrant) och den är
utgångspunkten. Varje avvikelse står utskriven med källa i § (4) *Vad jag bytte i planen*.

---

## catalogue-select

`python scripts/catalogue/sweep_raw.py` kördes om av mig innan urvalet:

```

EXIT=0

`python scripts/catalogue/select.py --brief tests/alunix-r8/runs/K4/BRIEF-draft.md --k 4 --wildcard --explain`,
hela utdatan ordagrant:

```
